Fluid dynamics foundations · Part 1

The Falling Apple and the Flowing Water

An illustrated, interactive introduction to the continuum hypothesis

About 9 minutes · 3 illustrations · 1 video · 2 interactive simulations

A simple question becomes a difficult problem

Imagine stepping out of a time machine into 1666. Beneath an apple tree sits a young Isaac Newton. You wait for the famous moment: an apple falls and strikes him on the head. But the apple lands a short distance away, on the grass. The familiar head injury is probably a legend; the important question is not.

Newton watches the apple fall. Why does it move downwards? For a solid object such as an apple, the problem is relatively straightforward. The apple has a definite shape, a recognisable boundary and a fixed mass. We can treat it as one body and describe its motion using Newton’s second law:

F = ma

Now imagine you are climbing onto a branch above Newton and pouring a bottle of water. The stream falls, stretches and changes shape as it moves. Newton can no longer point to one clearly bounded object and follow it as he followed the apple. How should he describe the motion of something that is continuously changing shape?

The puzzle becomes even harder if we zoom in. What looks to us like a smooth stream is, at the molecular scale, a vast collection of separate water molecules in constant motion. They collide, exchange momentum and energy, and are separated by tiny molecular-scale distances. A stream that appears continuous to our eyes is not literally continuous at this scale.

Why not follow every molecule?

One possible approach would be to apply the laws of mechanics to every molecule and then calculate how all their motions combine to produce the falling stream. In practice, this is not a workable way to describe an ordinary flow. Even a tiny amount of water contains an enormous number of molecules. Tracking the position, velocity and collisions of every one of them would be computationally overwhelming for most fluid-flow problems.

Fluid mechanics avoids this problem through a powerful modelling assumption: the continuum hypothesis. Instead of representing water as separate molecules with gaps between them, we treat it as a continuous substance. We assume that properties such as density, velocity, pressure and temperature can be defined smoothly at every position and time.

This is an approximation, not a claim that molecules or molecular gaps do not exist. It is a way of describing the collective behaviour of an enormous number of molecules without tracking each one individually.

Turning the flowing water into imaginary fluid parcels

Imagine water flowing continuously through a pipe. Although the water appears to be a single, connected stream, we can take our imagination a step further and divide it into many tiny portions. We call these portions fluid parcels. Think of each parcel as a tiny water apple, surrounded by an imaginary, well-defined boundary. These boundaries do not physically exist; they simply help us isolate and study small portions of the flowing water.

But how small should these imaginary water apples be? Each parcel must be small enough to represent the local properties of the flow, yet large enough to contain billions of water molecules. Although these molecules are constantly moving and colliding with one another, their random motions average out within the parcel. This allows us to assign meaningful average properties to each parcel, such as density, velocity, pressure and temperature.

Now, we can study how each imaginary water apple moves through the pipe and interacts with its neighbours. The water is driven by pressure differences, while viscosity influences how neighbouring layers of water move relative to one another. By applying the fundamental principles of conservation of mass, momentum and energy to these imaginary parcels, we can develop mathematical equations that describe the flow of the entire fluid, including the famous Navier–Stokes equations.

But this raises an important question: How small should we make these imaginary water apples to represent the flowing water accurately?

Finding the right size: the Representative Elementary Volume

The parcel cannot be reduced to a mathematical point, because a point may not contain a representative sample of molecules. Nor can it be made too large, because it would combine regions of the flow that may have different velocities, temperatures or pressures. Fluid mechanics therefore uses the idea of a Representative Elementary Volume (REV): a finite volume large enough to provide stable averaged properties, yet small enough to represent the local flow.

The REV sits between three distinct length scales:

  • Microscopic scale: the molecular spacing in a liquid, or the mean free path of gas molecules—the average distance a molecule travels between collisions. A volume that is too close to this scale contains too few molecules for reliable averages.

  • Mesoscopic scale: the size of the representative fluid parcel. It contains a very large number of molecules, so their random motions average out, while remaining small compared with the flow structures being studied.

  • Macroscopic flow scale: the characteristic size of the flow or of the feature of interest, such as the width of a water jet, the thickness of a boundary layer, the diameter of an eddy or the height of an ocean wave. A parcel that is too large would blur important spatial variations.

Molecular scale ≪ REV scale ≪ Flow scale

The symbol ≪ means ‘much smaller than’. The separation between these scales creates a range in which the REV can be both statistically representative and locally small. That is the ‘just right’ size needed for continuum modelling.

When does the continuum approximation work?

The next question is whether a fluid can always be treated as continuous. The answer is no. The validity of the approximation depends on how the molecular scale compares with the characteristic length of the flow. This comparison is expressed by the dimensionless Knudsen number:

Kn = λ / L

Here, λ is the molecular mean free path and L is a characteristic length of the flow. A small Knudsen number means that molecules collide with one another many times over a distance comparable with the flow scale. Their collective behaviour can then be represented by smooth, averaged properties. As Kn increases, molecular effects become increasingly important.

The characteristic length is not always simply the overall size of the system. A flow may occupy a vast region while one of its properties changes sharply over a very short distance. In that case, the relevant scale is the local gradient length, often expressed for a property Q as:

LQ ≈ Q / |∇Q|

For example, density may change rapidly across a shock wave. Even if the surrounding atmosphere is enormous, the shock itself has a very small characteristic length. The local gradient scale, rather than the size of the atmosphere, determines whether the continuum approximation remains valid there.

Four flow regimes: from a smooth fluid to individual molecules

As the Knudsen number grows, the flow passes through four commonly recognised regimes. The boundaries are approximate and can vary with the application, but the following ranges provide a useful guide.

  • Continuum flow (Kn < 0.001): Molecule-to-molecule collisions dominate. A fluid parcel contains enough molecules to have well-defined average properties, and the continuum description works well. The falling stream in Newton’s orchard, ocean currents, atmospheric winds, blood flow in arteries and most conventional aircraft flows are examples. The classical Navier–Stokes equations are generally applicable, together with the usual boundary conditions.

  • Slip flow (0.001 ≲ Kn < 0.1): The bulk of the gas can still be described as a continuum, but molecular effects become important close to solid boundaries. In a thin region near a wall—the Knudsen layer—molecules do not exchange momentum with neighbouring molecules frequently enough to enforce the usual no-slip condition. A small velocity slip and a temperature jump may occur at the surface. Navier–Stokes equations can still be used with suitable slip boundary conditions. Examples include gas flow through micro-scale devices and very small pores.

  • Transition flow (0.1 ≲ Kn < 10): Molecule–molecule collisions and molecule–wall collisions are both important. The assumption of a smooth local average becomes unreliable, so the conventional continuum formulation is no longer adequate. Molecular distribution functions must be considered, for example through the Boltzmann equation, or by particle-based approaches such as Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC). This regime can occur in rarefied high-altitude flows and vacuum-system components.

  • Free-molecular flow (Kn ≳ 10): Molecules travel long distances without colliding with one another. Interactions with solid surfaces become more important than interactions within the gas. The idea of a continuous fluid loses its usefulness, and the motion of individual molecules must be considered. Examples include very high-vacuum environments and parts of the flow around satellites in low Earth orbit.

A final distinction: continuum physics is not the same as a smooth-looking flow

A common misunderstanding is to associate the continuum hypothesis with calm or orderly motion. A flow can be highly turbulent and still behave as a continuum. When the falling stream hits the ground, it may break into splashes, vortices and rapidly changing structures. Those motions are complicated, but the turbulent eddies are generally still enormously larger than molecular scales.

The same is true in ocean and atmospheric modelling. Numerical models divide the domain into grid cells and represent the evolution of properties such as velocity, temperature and pressure. Turbulence may contain a wide range of eddy sizes, down to the Kolmogorov microscale in many flows. These turbulent scales are ordinarily far larger than molecular scales, so the continuum description remains valid even when the flow is chaotic.

The numerical grid size, the size of a fluid parcel used to define continuum properties, and the size of turbulent eddies are different concepts. A model grid cell is a computational choice; the REV is a physical averaging concept; and an eddy is a structure in the flow. Keeping these scales distinct is essential when interpreting numerical simulations.

Why the idea matters

The continuum hypothesis is what allows fluid mechanics to connect molecular behaviour with the equations used in engineering, atmospheric science and oceanography. Once density, velocity, pressure and temperature are treated as continuous fields, calculus can describe how they vary in space and time. Differential operators such as the material derivative, divergence and vorticity become meaningful, and macroscopic properties such as viscosity and thermal conductivity can be incorporated into governing equations.

Return, finally, to Newton’s orchard. The apple is a single body whose motion can be followed directly. The falling water is different: it is a collective of countless molecules, changing shape and interacting continuously. By treating that molecular crowd as a continuum—and by examining it through appropriately sized fluid parcels—we can describe its motion without following every molecule.

The continuum hypothesis is therefore not an attempt to deny the microscopic nature of matter. It is a carefully chosen bridge between two worlds: the restless motion of molecules and the large-scale flows we can observe, measure and model. It works remarkably well across most everyday and geophysical flows, but the Knudsen number reminds us where that bridge begins to narrow—and where, in rarefied or extremely small-scale environments, we must return to molecular physics.

Key idea to remember

A fluid can be treated as continuous when the molecular scale is far smaller than the scale of the flow.
